results.summary_before: FazyRV-ExoTiny is a minimal System-on-Chip based on the FazyRV RISC-V core that uses external QSPI ROM and RAM for program storage and data memory. It converts Wishbone bus accesses into QSPI transfers, enabling continuous mode for the ROM to reduce latency, and supports Quad Mode for the RAM. The design requires external QSPI flash and RAM chips, such as the W25Q128JV and APS6404L-3SQR, and careful reset synchronization; its implementation is near the edge of timing convergence.
results.summary: This design implements a Full Speed USB communications device class (CDC) device with two virtual serial ports. It is based on an existing USB CDC repository and appears to a PC as two COM ports, each with a different application. Testing requires a 48 MHz clock, a USB cable, a 1.5k resistor, and a computer, with optional buttons for inputs. A silicon test report confirms that the device enumerated as two serial ports and that each input sent a capital then lower case letter.

results.summary_before: This design is a simple UART transmitter that continuously sends a fixed set of strings on four separate output pins. The clock input is used directly to set the baud rate, so applying a 115200 Hz clock yields 115200 baud. It is tested by connecting one of the outputs to an asynchronous serial receiver. No external hardware beyond a serial port is required, and the documentation is very short.
results.summary: This design is an 8½ bit retro console with sprite and tile graphics plus a synthesizer. The PPU generates a stream of pixels for VGA output based on tile graphics, map, sprite data, and palette registers. The synth context-switches between voices at 96 kHz to produce audio samples. Testing requires an RP2040 RAM emulator and a VGA Pmod, with sound output left to the RP2040.
